verdict: Same five colours, same paper, same ink — B just can't tell a noun from a verb. It paints 'spot' red inside 'helps you spot weak verbs' while colouring every other bare infinitive on the page blue, then drops 'repetitions' and 'clutter' into body ink entirely and calls 'Check' a verb. states.name: all-dark
states.gap: Four words carry the wrong Category ink: 'repetitions' and 'clutter' are left in body grey #CCCCCC instead of noun red #CE896D; 'spot' — a verb in 'helps you spot weak verbs' — is painted noun red #CE896D where A gives it verb blue #829EBF; and in the proper noun 'Style Check', 'Style' is red but 'Check' is blue #829EBF, splitting one name across two Categories one line after B itself painted 'Syntax Highlight' red in full.
states.gapTheirs: Line pitch is not constant: baselines land at y=74/147/220/294, i.e. 73px, 73px, then 74px, so the fourth line sits 1px off the grid, where B holds a uniform 74px advance on all three gaps (x-height identical at 22px in both).
states.verdict: Both apps draw from the same five hexes — red CE896D, blue 829EBF, yellow B99558, green 89A474, purple B490B0 — so this is not a palette argument, it is a parsing argument, and B loses it. On the one line that matters B calls the verb 'spot' a noun and then fails to call the nouns 'repetitions' and 'clutter' anything at all, which is worse than no highlighting: a writer scanning for weak verbs is handed a red word that is a verb and a grey word that is a noun. B then breaks its own rule inside a line, painting 'Style' red and 'Check' blue after having painted 'Syntax Highlight' red end to end. A's only sin is a 1px stagger in the leading that nobody will notice; B's sins are the ones the feature exists to avoid.

states.name: focus-sentence
states.gap: A miscategorises 'Check' in the focus sentence: it paints it verb-blue #4776B5 — pixel-identical to the blue on 'll and 'make' — while B paints it noun-red #BC542E, the same red as the 'Style' beside it. Same word, same sentence, a whole Category apart, and it splits the capitalised pair 'Style Check' into red+blue mid-phrase; 1 of 8 coloured tokens (12.5%) is wrong. A also shows no caret anywhere in the frame — zero insertion-point pixels against B's 6x74px bar.
states.gapTheirs: B's caret is a 6px-wide, 74px-tall slab of #36BFFA that fills the entire line box (y169-242, i.e. the full 73px leading, not the text height) and butts flush against the 'e' of 'more' with 0px sidebearing. That cyan is more chromatic than any of the five Category colours on the page — it out-shouts the #BC542E noun red it sits three words from — so the loudest thing in a colour-coded sentence is a piece of furniture. B's type is also 1.4% tighter (advance 25.7px vs 26.0, line pitch 73px vs 74).
states.verdict: Everything that matters here is identical — same 52px left margin, same first-cap top at y=44, same five hues within 2/255, same dead-neutral #C4C4C4 dim on the two faded rows (max channel spread 4-5, no colour leaking through), same clean contraction split with the apostrophe of it'll carried into verb blue — so the whole judgement lands on one word. A calls the noun 'Check' a verb and tears a capitalised feature name in half, red then blue, which is exactly the lie that kills Syntax Highlight: if it invents a verb inside a proper name, you stop trusting it to find your real weak ones. B gets the word right and hands you a caret you can actually see, even if that caret is a fat cyan slab jammed against the 'e'. A garish caret you can retune in an afternoon; a tagger that colours nouns blue makes the whole feature furniture.
